# Autoencoder
An autoencoder is composed of two functions: an encoder that maps input data from a high-dimensional space to a lower-dimensional latent code, and a decoder that reconstructs the original input from this code. Both the encoder and decoder are typically multilayer perceptrons. Training an autoencoder involves minimizing the reconstruction error (often L2 loss) between the original data and its reconstruction, using a dataset that serves as the reference distribution. Undercomplete autoencoders (where latent space has fewer dimensions than input) compress information and prevent the trivial identity mapping; overcomplete variants may still learn useful features.
Variants of autoencoders include sparse autoencoders, which encourage sparsity in latent representations; denoising autoencoders, trained to reconstruct clean inputs from corrupted ones; contractive autoencoders, which penalize sensitivity to small input changes; variational autoencoders (VAE), which model the latent space as probabilistic distributions; concrete autoencoders for feature selection; and minimum description length autoencoders, which optimize information-theoretic principles. Autoencoders are used for dimensionality reduction, information retrieval, anomaly detection, image processing, machine translation, drug discovery, and more. With deep architectures, autoencoders achieve better compression and feature learning. Their development began in the 1980s, with principal component analysis as a linear precursor and many extensions used in modern AI systems.
